24035-the-pirates-of-ersatz:
Murray Leinster's The Pirates of Ersatz opens with a motto: sometimes nobody loves a benefactor, least of all on a rich, self-satisfied planet. Grandpa always held pirates to be benefactors in truth, and Bron Hoddan sets out to prove it.

Hoddan stows away on a ship that arrived to execute all his relatives, a plan long cherished and carefully worked out. His relatives will act grieved and innocent, prove blameless lives, and shame their executioners, then return to piracy when the strangers leave. Hoddan aims for Walden, the most civilized world in that region of the galaxy, to become an electronic engineer, grow rich, marry a delightful girl, and end a great man. It takes two years to arrange even the first.
32584-the-secret-of-kralitz:
Henry Kuttner's The Secret of Kralitz, printed in Weird Tales in October 1936, opens with a midnight summons in a castle. Black-swathed guides lead the narrator, heir to the Barons Kralitz, down a hidden stairway to an underground cavern. There he expects at last to learn the family secret his dying father would not name.

That secret reaches back to the first Baron, who burned a monastery, slew its monks, and took a girl the abbot had sheltered. The dying abbot cursed the slayer and his sons for unborn generations, and the tale builds its horror on what that curse means for the eldest son of each generation.
7564-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-c:
Cardinal de Retz, the Fronde conspirator and archbishop, wrote memoirs that are a masterclass in political cunning, and this volume gathers their quotations and images. Always judged of actions by men, and never men by their actions, one maxim says. Always to sacrifice the little affairs to the greater is another. Arms not tempered by laws quickly become anarchy.

Assurance often supplies the room of good sense, and blindness makes authority consist only in force. Buckingham had been in love with three queens, and civil war, Retz warns, is one of those complicated diseases not powerful enough to conclude a peace. The collection gives the Fronde in epigrams: patience joined with activity, bounty that echoes louder for being secret, and ambition measured in pistoles and promises.
britannica-1911-berlichingen-goetz:
Goetz von Berlichingen (1480–1562), a German knight born at Jagsthausen in Württemberg, is the subject of this 1911 Britannica biography. After early service under the Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach and the emperor Maximilian I, he raised a company of freelances and fought in a string of private wars across Germany.

Losing his right hand at the siege of Landshut in 1505, he fought on with an iron hand kept at Jagsthausen. The entry follows his feuds, ransoms, bans under the empire, and captivity at Heilbronn, and closes with his lasting fame through Goethe's 1773 play and his own autobiography.
britannica-1911-bielitz:
Bielitz, called Bilsko in Czech and Bielsko in Polish, is a town of Austrian Silesia. It lies 80 miles south-east of Troppau by rail, on the Biala river. Across the river stands the Galician town of Biala. The population in 1900 was 16,885, chiefly German. A fine castle of the Sulkowsky family stands in the town. Their lordship of Bielitz was raised to a duchy in 1752.

Woollen and linen making lead the town's industry. Jute and machinery works also operate there. The 1911 Britannica entry stresses an active export trade in woollens, aimed especially at the East. The town was founded in the 13th century. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was a fortified place. The entry is short, with geography, castle, and cloth trade as its three points.
britannica-1911-carriere-moritz:
Moritz Carrière (1817–1895) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a German philosopher and historian born at Griedel in Hesse-Darmstadt. He studied at Giessen, Göttingen, and Berlin, then spent some years in Italy studying the fine arts. In 1842 he settled at Giessen as a teacher of philosophy. In 1853 he became professor at Munich, where he lectured mainly on aesthetics.

Carrière stood as an open enemy of Ultramontanism and helped make German unity welcome to South Germans. He followed the younger Fichte's school, holding a theistic view that tried to reconcile deism and pantheism, a position he called “real-idealism.” His chief works include the Aesthetik of 1859 and a large study of art within the growth of culture. He also wrote on the philosophy of the Reformation age and on the moral order of the world, holding both fixed natural law and free will.
britannica-1911-chemnitz:
Chemnitz is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Saxony. It stands 50 miles west south west of Dresden and 51 miles south east of Leipzig by rail. Its population in 1905 was 244,405. It lies 950 feet above the sea, in a fertile plain at the foot of the Erzgebirge. The river Chemnitz, a tributary of the Mulde, waters it. It is the chief manufacturing town in the kingdom.

The old inner town is ringed by promenades on the site of its fortifications. Beyond them lies industrial Chemnitz, a thick belt of streets and factories. The market square holds the medieval Rathaus and monuments to William I, Bismarck, and Moltke. The town's industry has earned it the name of “Saxon Manchester.” Its locomotive and engineering works come first. They employ some 20,000 hands in ninety factories. The entry presents a city remade by its own machines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnetz: Agnetz, from Latin agnus, lamb, is the Slavonic word for the square bread portion cut from the first loaf when preparing for Mass according to the Greek rite. That preparation is called the proskomide. The word is used in Byzantine Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches in the United States as well as Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-max:
Alexander Maximilian Seitz was a German painter, born at Munich in 1811 and dead at Rome in 1888. Cornelius taught him; Joseph Sold by His Brethren and the Seven Sleepers, two early pictures, won quick recognition. Heinrich Hess gave him work on the All Saints frescoes. After he painted four of the sacraments, Cornelius brought him to Rome, where he found a kindred spirit in Overbeck.

Seitz helped Overbeck with the frescoes of the Evangelists and Apostles at Castel Gandolfo and, with his gifted son Ludwig, later completed Overbeck's frescoes at Diakovár cathedral. With his son he also painted a cycle of saints for Herder of Freiburg. Besides scenes of Roman common life, he treated chiefly Old and New Testament subjects. These included the Adoration of the Shepherds, Christ as the Friend of Children, and the Finding of Moses, all in Overbeck's spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalarius-of-:
Amalarius of Metz, liturgical writer born at Metz late in the eighth century, died about 850. Long thought distinct from Amalarius of Trèves, he is now held to have become Bishop of Trèves about 811, by Dom Morin's researches. He left after two years as envoy to Constantinople. Alcuin's disciple, he later attended synods at Aix-la-Chapelle and Paris.

He served Louis le Débonnaire as ambassador to Gregory IV, and governed Lyons during Agobard's exile, where Florus opposed his antiphonary. Censured at Quierzy in 838 over the divided Host, later drawn into Gottschalk's predestination controversies, he wrote on liturgy. His De ecclesiasticis officiis explains Mass, Office, benedictions, ordinations, vestments, seasons from Septuagesima to Pentecost, and Holy Week. His De ordine antiphonarii explains the Office's arrangement and the antiphons' origin, and defends his compilation from Rome's and Metz's antiphonaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-de-r:
Cardinal de Retz, Archbishop of Paris, was born at the Château of Montmirail in October 1614 and died in Paris in August 1679. Destined for the Church though he said it suited neither his taste nor his temper, he learned seven languages. Reading Plutarch and Sallust gave him a taste for republican maxims and conspiracy. At eighteen he wrote on the conspiracy of Fieschi, approving what his model Mascardi had blamed.

After plots against Richelieu and consecration as coadjutor in 1644, he won Paris by sermons and reform of priests, then opposed Mazarin through the Fronde years. Arrested by Louis XIV's order in December 1652, he later resigned the see in 1662 for the Abbey of St. Denis, whose income doubled the archbishopric's. He figured in the conclaves that chose Clement IX and Clement X, and his memoirs, begun in 1671, first appeared in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-mansuet:
César-Mansuete Despretz was a chemist and physicist born at Lessines, Belgium, on 11 May 1798 and dying at Paris on 11 May 1863. Early in life he became master of studies at the Bruges lyceum, then went to Paris, where Gay-Lussac had him made tutor of the chemical course at the Ecole Polytechnique. In 1824 he became professor of physics at the Collège Henri IV, and in 1837 took the physics chair at the Sorbonne.

Naturalized French in 1838, he entered the Academy of Sciences in 1841 as successor of Savart. His researches helped lay the foundations of modern physics, above all in heat. He studied latent heat in 1818 and heat conduction in 1821. An Academy-crowned memoir on animal heat followed in 1822, then liquid compressibility in 1823 and gas density in 1827, which showed Mariotte's law did not hold exactly for gases. He died a devout Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-muentz:
Eugene Muentz was a French savant and historian, born at Soulz-sous-Forêts, near Mülhausen, Alsace, on 11 June 1845 and dead at Paris on 2 November 1902. He studied law, but turned to the Revue Alsacienne, where his articles caused much comment. Just then attention was being directed in France to the study of history. Albert Dumont founded the École Française at Rome, and Müntz became one of its pupils.

Louis Duchesne, director of the school, was a fellow-student. Müntz explored the Vatican Archives and Library, amassing the erudition he revealed in later years. From that time he devoted himself to unravelling the history of art in Italy. About 1880, with Morelli and Milanesi, he contributed immensely to this study, applying the positive method of inquiry. Müntz's work rests on acquaintance with original documents: archive papers, memoranda, bills, inventories, and contracts, supported by knowledge of monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-dum:
Francisco Dumetz, a native of Majorca whose birth date is unknown and who died on 14 January 1811. He was the last of the Franciscan friars of California, toiling there without interruption for forty years. He entered the Franciscan order in Majorca and in May 1770 sailed to Mexico with forty-eight other Franciscans for the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico City. Volunteering for the Indian missions, he was posted to California in October 1770.

Sailing from San Blas with ten friars in January 1771, he arrived at Monterey in May and was assigned to Mission San Diego. He then went to San Carlos in 1772 and San Buenaventura in 1782, where he laboured for the Indians until 1797. Directed to found Mission San Fernando, he stayed there from its founding on 8 September 1797 to the end of 1805, apart from two years at San Gabriel. He served there from 1806 until his death and burial in the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-von-st:
Johann von Staupitz was the Augustinian leader who first guided Martin Luther and later refused to follow him. Born in Saxony about 1460, he studied at Leipzig, joined the Augustinians, and became prior at Tubingen and doctor of theology in 1500. In 1503 he was elected vicar-general of the German Augustinians and became the first dean of theology at the new University of Wittenberg.

At Erfurt he had consoled the young Luther, tormented by his sinfulness, with talk of God's forgiving grace, and Luther stayed grateful for it. Sent in 1518 to remonstrate with Luther, Staupitz hesitated, released him from obedience to the order, and forwarded his explanation to Rome. When Rome demanded a retraction in 1520, he declared the pope his judge, joined the Benedictines, and ended as Abbot of St. Peter's at Salzburg, Catholic in doctrine to the last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-maria-:
Joseph Maria von Radowitz was a Prussian general, diplomat, and Catholic statesman. Born at Blankenburg in 1797 of Hungarian descent, he fought with the French in the Wars of Liberation, then served Hesse and, from 1823, Prussia. Raised among Protestants, he became a strong Catholic through study of the Incarnation and the Church's founding.

Rejecting both liberalism and absolutism, Radowitz followed Haller in favoring government by Estates. He improved Prussian artillery, wrote for the Politische Wochenblatt, and served as military attaché at Frankfurt and ambassador to south German courts. After 1840, Frederick William IV often called him to Berlin for advice on German reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-caramuel:
Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz was a Spanish Cistercian prodigy who wrote on nearly everything. Born at Madrid in 1606, he published astronomical tables at ten, learned Asian tongues including Chinese, and joined the Cistercians at La Espina. He earned a Louvain doctorate in 1638, led armed clerics defending Prague from the Swedes in 1648, and ended as Bishop of Vigevano.

Caramuel published, by one count, 262 works on grammar, poetry, mathematics, astronomy, physics, politics, canon law, and theology. Little of it lasts, and his attempt to solve moral theology by mathematical rules won him St. Alphonsus' title Prince of the Laxists. The entry marvels at his range and judges his substance thin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-koniggratz:
Koniggratz is a Bohemian diocese founded to replace Leitomischl, lost in the Hussite wars. Emperor Ferdinand III secured the Chrast estate and Auretitz manor from Countess Anna Eusebia von Harrach, and Alexander VII's bull of erection dates to 10 November 1664.

Matthias Ferdinand Zoubek von Bilenberg, abbot of St. Nikolaus in Prague, became first bishop. The see first covered only the Koniggratz district, then gained Chrudim and Czaslau from Prague in 1784 under Joseph II. By late 1909 it counted 1,476,942 Catholics, 998 secular priests, 404 parishes served by secular clergy, and 16 served by orders, in a mostly Czech population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leitmeritz:
Leitmeritz, in Austria, covers northern Bohemia. After Christianity came under Charlemagne and Louis the German, its ground belonged to Ratisbon diocese, until Otto I founded Prague in 973 for all Bohemia. Leitmeritz's first church, St. Wenceslaus, rose in 925, and Duke Spitihnew built St. Stephen's and a collegiate chapter in 1057.

By 1384 the city with suburbs held thirteen churches and chapels, many religious, and twenty secular priests in the cure of souls. Hussite wars wrecked that flourishing order: Ziska spared Leitmeritz in 1421 only for accepting Hussitism, and the despoiled collegiate church alone kept communion under one kind. Hussitism prepared Protestantism, which Luther's teaching spread through nobles enriched by church wealth and priest Gallus Cahera's preaching. The Thirty Years War reversed the tide, and Harrach split Prague to create Koniggratz and Leitmeritz, whose first bishop, Max Rudolf von Schleinitz, took office in 1655.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lutzk-zhitomi:
Lutzk, Zhitomir, and Kamenetz form one diocese in Little Russia, spanning Volhynia, Kiev, and Podolia. Three old sees merged under Russian pressure on Rome, meant to tighten state grip on the Church, and the bishop at Zhitomir rules with three auxiliaries, two sees now vacant.

Greek Rite first, the land turned Latin as Lithuanians took Volhynia in 1320 and Poles united Lithuania in 1569. Lutzk, founded in 1358 at Vladimir and moved to Lutzk in 1428, hosted six provincial synods and 183 churches in the eighteenth century. Cyril Terletzki of Lutzk signed first for union at Brest in 1590, and Volhynia passed to Russia in 1792.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-josephi:
Josephine Goetz was second superior-general of the Society of the Sacred Heart, born in 1817 and dead in 1874. Her parents died early, and an aunt schooled her at the Sacred Heart convent in Besancon.

At seventeen she entered the Sacred Heart novitiate at Montet and took first vows in 1837. In 1842 she took charge of the troubled Besancon school, and her shrewd management marked her for higher office. After profession in 1847 she became mistress of novices at Conflans, later also superior of the house, until named vicar-general in 1864. On foundress Madeleine Sophie Barat's death she was elected superior-general in 1865. For nine years she consolidated and developed the foundress's work, founding a Conflans training school for young teachers and revising the curriculum by committee. Visitations across Europe followed until paralysis killed her after a few days' illness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metz:
Metz, a town and bishopric in Lorraine, was known in ancient times as Divodurum, capital of the Celtic Mediomatrici, already held by Rome at the Christian era's start. One of the last strongholds to yield to the Germans, it survived Hun attacks and passed peacefully to the Franks near the fifth century's end.

Theodorick of Austrasia chose it as his residence in 511, and Queen Brunhild's reign shed great splendour on the town. Though the first Christian churches stood outside the city, the fifth-century oratory of St. Stephen inside the walls is fully proven. In the seventh century's start the oldest monasteries were St. Glossinde and St. Peter. Under the Carolingians the town kept the rulers' favour, their family seat lying nearby. Charles the Bald was crowned in the Basilica, and Louis the Pious and his son Drogo lie buried there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olmutz:
Olomouc, an archdiocese in Moravia, guards the legacy of Cyril and Methodius in Slavic Christianity. Christianity reached Moravia by the fourth century, Huns and Avars wiped it out, and Prince Rastislav asked the Greek emperor, not the Franks, for missionaries.

Michael III sent Cyril and Methodius, who invented the Glagolitic alphabet, translated the Bible into Slavic, and won Adrian II's leave to use Slavic in worship. German clergy opposed them, yet Methodius became archbishop of Pannonia and Moravia, and the entry follows Olomouc's bishops to modern times. Cyril died in a Roman monastery; Methodius, meanwhile, rose to archbishop of Pannonia and Moravia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-aloys-g:
Peter Aloys Gratz was a Bavarian schoolmaster and biblical scholar, born at Mittelberg in 1769. Schooled by monks at Füssen and in classics at Augsburg, he entered the Dillingen seminary in 1788 and was ordained in 1792. Parish work at Unterthalheim left him time to write textbooks for elementary schools and to pursue New Testament study, the field that made his name.

In 1812 he argued that a Hebrew original lay behind one of the Synoptic Gospels, and the work's learning won him chairs in Greek and biblical interpretation at Ellwangen that same year. Freiburg gave him a theology doctorate in 1813. He published studies of Justin's memoirs and of interpolations in Paul's letters, and later taught at Bonn. He died at Darmstadt in 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-fritz:
Samuel Fritz, an eighteenth-century Jesuit famed for mapping the Amazon, was born at Trautenau in Bohemia in 1654 and died on 20 March 1728. Joining the Society in 1673, he was sent to Quito in 1684 and spent forty-two years among the Indians of the Upper Marañón. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia celebrates a missionary who was also a craftsman, linguist, and mapmaker.

He converted the powerful Omaguas and gathered peoples from forty settlements between the Napo and Negro rivers into ordered towns. Skilled with his hands and quick with languages, he knew by instinct how to deal with native peoples, winning respect from Indians and Spaniards alike. At Quito's high court's request he began in 1687 to chart the disputed Amazon country, work that served Spain in its boundary quarrel with Portugal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-arnulf-of-:
St. Arnulf of Metz was a statesman and bishop under the Merovingians, born about 580. He died about 640. This entry follows a boy of a distinguished Frankish family living in Austrasia, the eastern section of Clovis's kingdom. In his boyhood school he excelled through talent and good behaviour. In due time, as custom required, he was sent to the court of Theodebert II, king of Austrasia from 595 to 612, to learn the branches of government.

Under Gundulf, mayor of the palace, he soon became so proficient that he joined the regular list of royal officers, among the first of the king's ministers. He distinguished himself as a military commander and in civil administration, at one time caring for six distinct provinces. In due course he married a Frankish woman of noble lineage, and she bore him two sons, Anseghisel and Clodulf.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trebnitz:
A former abbey of Cistercian nuns north of Breslau in Silesia, founded in 1203 by Duke Henry the Bearded and his wife St. Hedwig. The foundation story says Henry, trapped in a swamp while hunting, vowed to build the abbey in return for rescue, and Hedwig's brother Bishop Ekbert of Bamberg chose its first nuns.

The first abbess was Petrussa, followed by Gertrude, Hedwig's daughter, and abbesses were Piast princesses, then noblewomen, until 1515. The house endured famine, repeated fires, flight to Poland in the Thirty Years War and again in 1663, until its last abbess died in 1810 and the abbey was suppressed that November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wenzel-anton-:
Wenzel Anton Kaunitz was an Austrian prince and statesman born at Vienna in 1711 and dying there in 1794. Destined by his parents for the Church, he held a Münster canonry by thirteen, but abandoned the clerical path, studied law at Vienna, Leipzig. Leyden, travelled for education through England and Italy, and became aulic councillor in 1735.

Diplomatic service followed swiftly. He served as imperial commissary at the Ratisbon diet in 1739, on missions to Florence, Rome, and Turin in 1741, and as ambassador at Turin in 1742. When Maurice de Saxe took Brussels after a three-week siege in February 1746, Kaunitz withdrew to Antwerp, then Aachen, until the empress granted his urgent recall that June. In 1748 he represented Austria at the Congress of Aachen.
nasa-tm-19700002181-snap-8-nak-pump-moto:
Fred Boecker of Lewis Research Center reports start tests for the SNAP-8 sodium-potassium pump motor assembly in this November 1969 memorandum. Two hermetically sealed induction motor pumps were tested in NaK loops. NaK, a sodium-potassium mixture, carries heat in the SNAP-8 space power system.

Tests checked starting on 400-hertz power across wide temperature ranges. Flow resistance was preset by a valve before each start, covering flow rates up to a high maximum. Both pumps started successfully at the hotter stator conditions reported. At colder stator temperatures, both pumps experienced startup difficulties. The pattern tells designers the thermal conditions a SNAP-8 pump needs for reliable starts.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-cardin:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Cardinal de Retz, prepared by David Widger, lifts short passages from the Cardinal's memoirs and arranges them in alphabetical order. Retz wrote from inside the plots and civil wars of seventeenth-century France, and the extracts carry his cool, worldly voice.

He judged actions by men, the first entries say, and never men by actions, and he sacrificed little affairs to greater ones. Civil war is called a complicated disease, not powerful enough to conclude a peace. Buckingham had been in love with three queens, arms untempered by laws quickly become anarchy, and contempt is named the most dangerous disease of any state.
